sourceNote: Status comes from Robert Garza’s public bill tracker, read on September 24, 2026. Passed means signed into law. In progress means a bill of this nature has been introduced. Not started means no bill yet.

bills.title: A New Start at Equality
bills.label: Presumed 50/50 Custody
bills.summary: Creates a rebuttable presumption of equal custody — the foundation of 50/50 custody laws and shared parenting legislation — giving every child the benefit of both parents and every custody case a fair starting point.

Alabama.note: similar bill, not this model draft

Arkansas.detail: Act 604 (Senate Bill 18, 2021) creates a rebuttable presumption that joint custody, an approximately equal division of time, is in the child’s best interest.

Florida.detail: House Bill 1301 (2023), effective July 1, 2023, creates a rebuttable presumption that equal time-sharing is in the child’s best interest.

Kentucky.detail: House Bill 528 (2018) creates a rebuttable presumption that joint custody and equally shared parenting time are in the child’s best interest.

Louisiana.detail: Act 605 (House Bill 1239), effective August 1, 2026, requires physical custody to be shared equally unless the court finds that is not feasible or not in the child’s best interest. It does not automatically change existing custody orders.

Maryland.note: similar bill, not this model draft

Mississippi.detail: House Bill 1662, signed in 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, creates a rebuttable presumption of joint custody with equal parenting time.

Missouri.detail: Senate Bill 35, signed in 2023, creates a rebuttable presumption that equal or approximately equal parenting time is in the child’s best interest.

West Virginia.detail: Senate Bill 463 (2022) creates a rebuttable presumption that an equal 50/50 custodial allocation is in the child’s best interest.

bills.title: Time Taken Time Back
bills.label: Restore lost parenting time after false accusations
bills.summary: Ensures that any parenting time lost due to false allegations in custody or unsubstantiated investigations is automatically restored, protecting non-custodial parent rights and the parent-child bond, and deterring the weaponization of the court system.

Texas.detail: Family Code §157.168 requires makeup possession when court-ordered time is denied, unless there is good cause not to order it. After three contempt findings for that child, the makeup time is twice what was denied.

Utah.detail: Senate Bill 304, signed March 23, 2026, requires make-up parent-time when a parent lost time because the other parent knowingly falsified information to obtain a protective order.

bills.title: Three Strikes Law
bills.label: Penalties for breaking custody orders
bills.summary: Creates escalating consequences for parents who repeatedly violate court-ordered custody — misdemeanor for the first two offenses, felony for the third — ensuring that custody orders are respected and children are protected from ongoing custody interference.

bills.title: Justice Delayed is Justice Denied
bills.label: 10-day ruling deadline
bills.summary: Requires family court judges to issue rulings within 10 business days of a hearing, with written justification required for any extension — because a custody case taking too long leaves families in legal limbo.

bills.title: Cameras in Courtrooms
bills.label: Every hearing recorded
bills.summary: Requires video and audio recording of all court proceedings — including off-the-record moments — to ensure family court transparency, protect litigants, and provide appellate courts with a complete record of what happened.

bills.title: Child Support Dual Calculation Reform
bills.label: Support offset by overnights
bills.summary: Modernizes child support calculations for 50/50 custody and shared parenting by requiring courts to compute each parent’s obligation based on actual overnight parenting time, offset the amounts, and order only the difference — ending inconsistent outcomes that assume one primary household.

Arizona.detail: Arizona’s child support guidelines give a parenting-time credit based on the number of days the child spends with each parent.

California.detail: Family Code §4055 counts the higher-earning parent’s share of time with the child in the support formula.

Colorado.detail: Section 14-10-115, when each parent has the child for more than 92 overnights, figures support for both parents and orders the difference.

Florida.detail: Section 61.30, when a child spends a substantial number of overnights with each parent, figures support for both parents and orders the difference.

Hawaii.detail: Hawaii’s 2024 child support guidelines use a separate worksheet for equal time-sharing and for a parent with more than 143 overnights, and the parent with the higher obligation pays the difference.

Illinois.detail: When each parent has the child for at least 146 overnights, the Marriage and Dissolution of Marriage Act figures support for both parents and orders the difference.

Indiana.detail: Indiana’s child support guidelines give a parenting-time credit based on the number of overnights the child spends with the parent who pays support.

Maryland.detail: Family Law §12-204, when each parent has the child for more than 25 percent of overnights, figures support for both parents and orders the difference.

South Carolina.detail: Regulation 114-4730, when each parent has the child for more than 109 overnights, figures support for both parents and orders the difference.

bills.title: The Litigant Access and Economy Act
bills.label: Right to appear remotely for court hearings
bills.summary: Guarantees a presumptive right to appear remotely in non-evidentiary family court hearings, protecting working parents and self-represented litigants from default judgments caused by inability to attend in person.

bills.title: Appealable Temporary Orders
bills.label: Temporary orders can be appealed
bills.summary: Creates a statutory right to a temporary custody order appeal for visitation and support — ending the practice of 'temporary' orders that function as permanent judgments without any appellate oversight.

Maryland.detail: Courts and Judicial Proceedings §12-303 allows an appeal before final judgment from an order that takes away or changes a parent’s custody, and from an order requiring payment of money, including temporary child support.

bills.title: Reimbursement of Fees for Parental Alienating Behaviors
bills.label: Alienating parent pays legal fees
bills.summary: Requires courts to order full reimbursement of attorney’s fees, therapy costs, and evaluator expenses when a parent is found to have engaged in alienating behavior — holding alienators financially accountable and funding the targeted parent’s path to reunification.

bills.title: The Family Rights and Due Process Act
bills.label: Clear and convincing evidence standard in family court
bills.summary: Raises the evidentiary standard in family court from ‘more likely than not’ to ‘clear and convincing evidence’ and requires judges to issue written findings for every ruling — ensuring that non-custodial parent rights and all fundamental parental rights are protected by rigorous, transparent decision-making.

bills.title: Child Support Integrity Act
bills.label: DNA testing before child support
bills.summary: Requires genetic verification of parentage before any child support order can be entered and provides immediate relief when later DNA testing proves non-parentage — protecting children, preventing wrongful obligations based on false allegations in custody, and restoring integrity to the child support system.

bills.title: Best Interest of the Child Definition Act
bills.label: Evidence-based best interest factors
bills.summary: Establishes a clear statutory definition of 'best interest of the child,' requiring courts to base custody decisions on evidence — not assumptions, speculation, or personal preference. Courts retain full authority to protect children from abuse, neglect, family violence, and harm; this definition ensures that authority is exercised consistently and reviewably across every state.

Maryland.detail: House Bill 1191, effective October 1, 2025, lists the factors a court may consider in deciding legal and physical custody and requires the court to state its findings.

bills.title: Parent-Child Restoration Act
bills.label: Restore time when claims fail
bills.summary: When allegations that led to temporary custody or visitation restrictions are not substantiated, families should not remain separated by unsupported orders. This act requires prompt restoration of the prior parenting arrangement and compensatory parenting time while preserving protections when clear and convincing evidence shows continued restrictions are necessary.
